2.3 Warning-model development and evalua:
The Seismic-bumps dataset and its binary label were retained with all 18 original predictors. The unchanged stratified 70:30 split (seed 42) allocated 1,808 records to training and 776 to held-out testing, including 51 positive and 725 negative test records. The categorical predictors were seismic, seismoacoustic, shift, ghazard. They were encoded with OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'). The numerical predictors were genergy, gpuls, gdenergy, gdpuls, nbumps, nbumps2, nbumps3, nbumps4, nbumps5, nbumps6, nbumps7, nbumps89, energy, maxenergy. StandardScaler was used for logistic regression (LR) and the support vector machine (SVM); numerical values were passed through unchanged for random forest (RF) and gradient boosting (GB). Preprocessing was fitted inside a Pipeline and ColumnTransformer using only each fitting subset. Missing values were verified absent, and no imputation was applied. All original predictors and estimator hyperparameters were retained without feature selection, PCA or hyperparameter search.

LR, RF and SVM used class_weight='balanced'. GB received compute_sample_weight('balanced', y_fit), calculated as n_fit/(2*n_class) using only the current fitting subset. Positive-class predict_proba outputs were evaluated using ROC-AUC and average precision, reported as PR-AUC. Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, true positives (TP), false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN) were evaluated at a reference decision cut-off of 0.5. Precision was defined as zero when no positive predictions were made. Brier score measured mean squared error of the positive-class score against the binary outcome. A cut-off of 0.5 was not interpreted as neutral, optimal or equivalent across models.

The actual revision runtime was Python 3.12.14 with numpy 2.5.1, pandas 3.0.3, scipy 1.18.0, scikit-learn 1.9.0, matplotlib 3.11.0, PyYAML 6.0.3, pytest 9.1.1, Pillow 12.3.0, imbalanced-learn 0.14.2. Historical frozen-v2 metadata recorded Python 3.12.13; that runtime was not retested in this extension. Complete original settings and actual deep pipeline parameters are supplied in S1 File and the code package.
2.4 Decision-cut-off and alert-burden an:
Each model was evaluated at decision cut-offs from 0.01 to 0.99, in increments of 0.01. Alert burden was defined as TP + FP within the 776-record held-out test set; false alarms were FP and missed hazardous cases were FN. Alert burden does not represent measured mine staffing or dispatch capacity. Model-specific cut-offs were not interpreted as calibrated absolute hazard probabilities. For matched-burden comparison, all tied scores were retained, and the jointly attainable alert count nearest the prespecified target of 150 was selected, with lower counts breaking distance ties. Alert counts and cut-offs were selected using model scores without labels; test labels were then used to evaluate performance.

Relative cost sensitivity used C = r_FN × FN + FP, with false-positive cost fixed at one and FN:FP ratios of 1:1, 2:1, 5:1, 10:1, 20:1, 50:1, 100:1. These ratios are hypothetical sensitivity scenarios and are not empirically measured mine-specific costs. Cost per test record was C/776. For each model and ratio, the minimum observed over the existing cut-off grid was reported as a descriptive minimum on the held-out test set. The lowest cut-off was used to display tied minima, and all tied cut-offs were retained. These label-dependent summaries are not optimal deployment thresholds or recommendations for mine practice; independent validation would be needed for threshold selection.
2.5 Robustness and sensitivity analysis:
RepeatedStratifiedKFold with 5 folds and 10 repeats (seed 42) was applied only within the fixed training subset. Each model therefore had 50 validation-fold results. Encoding, scaling and weighting were refitted using only each fold's training records; GB sample weights were recomputed from those training labels. Mean ROC-AUC and PR-AUC were summarized with sample SD (ddof = 1). Fold SD describes dispersion across overlapping resplits and is not a confidence interval based on independent experiments. The held-out test set did not participate in cross-validation.

Paired stratified bootstrap sampling used the unchanged held-out predictions, 2,000 resamples and seed 42. Each resample drew 51 positive and 725 negative records with replacement, using identical indices for all models. Percentile intervals at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles were computed for ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, recall, precision and Brier score. Recall and precision used the reference cut-off of 0.5. No-positive-prediction cases were explicitly flagged, with precision set to zero. Intervals are conditional on the fitted models and the held-out class composition; they do not include model-development or site-level uncertainty.

RandomOverSampler was included as a sensitivity analysis rather than as the primary modeling strategy. An imbalanced-learn Pipeline applied training-fitted preprocessing, RandomOverSampler(sampling_strategy='auto', random_state=42, shrinkage=None), and the original estimator. To avoid double correction, LR, RF and SVM used class_weight=None in this arm, and GB received no balanced sample weights. The sampler duplicated training records without synthesizing values and never accessed held-out or validation records. The same held-out split and repeated training-only cross-validation splits were used. Ordinary SMOTE was not adopted because the dataset contains mixed categorical and continuous predictors and the purpose was to avoid introducing synthetic category combinations without a dedicated mixed-data synthesis design.

Calibration curves used ten quantile bins with tied scores retained together and empty bins omitted. No new post-hoc calibration model was fitted. Paired DeLong tests evaluated differences in ROC-AUC, and exact McNemar tests evaluated discordant classification correctness on the same records at the common alert count. Holm correction was applied separately to the six comparisons in each family. These row-level methods assume exchangeable records; the data lack reliable site/time grouping information and do not establish temporal or external generalization.
3.1 Revised warning-model performance:
The revised held-out results are reported in Table 4 and Fig 4. LR had ROC-AUC 0.783, PR-AUC 0.214 and Brier score 0.172. RF had ROC-AUC 0.762, PR-AUC 0.244 and Brier score 0.064. GB had ROC-AUC 0.751, PR-AUC 0.258 and Brier score 0.110. SVM had ROC-AUC 0.696, PR-AUC 0.170 and Brier score 0.059.

At the reference cut-off, LR yielded TP/FP/FN = 32/134/19, recall 0.627 and alert burden 166; RF yielded TP/FP/FN = 8/18/43, recall 0.157 and alert burden 26; GB yielded TP/FP/FN = 21/83/30, recall 0.412 and alert burden 104; SVM yielded TP/FP/FN = 0/0/51, recall 0.000 and alert burden 0. The different metric and operating-point comparisons do not establish a universally superior model.
3.2 Decision-cut-off and matched-alert-b:
The four-model grid contained 396 model–cut-off combinations (Fig 5; S3 Table). At the common attained burden of 147 alerts (Table 5), recall was LR 0.627, RF 0.549, GB 0.510, SVM 0.392. The corresponding precision values were LR 0.218, RF 0.190, GB 0.177, SVM 0.136. The full attainable-count comparisons are shown in S2 Fig.

The hypothetical cost scenarios produced the descriptive held-out minima in S6 Table and S3 Fig. For FN:FP = 10:1, LR had minimum cost 292 at cut-off 0.55 with 102 FP and 19 FN; RF had minimum cost 345 at cut-off 0.15 with 185 FP and 16 FN; GB had minimum cost 360 at cut-off 0.29 with 200 FP and 16 FN; SVM had minimum cost 402 at cut-off 0.12 with 62 FP and 34 FN. These are descriptive minima selected on the evaluated records, not independently validated deployment recommendations.
3.3 Calibration, repeated cross-validati:
Four-model calibration curves are shown in S1 Fig. The LR fixed-width diagnostic retained a local decrease in observed positive fraction, from 10/185 (0.054) in the (0.300, 0.400] bin to 3/88 (0.034) in (0.400, 0.500]. Calibration was not assumed to be monotonic, and a smaller Brier score alone did not establish better safety-warning performance.

Training-only repeated cross-validation yielded ROC-AUC mean ± SD of LR 0.744 ± 0.054, RF 0.719 ± 0.051, GB 0.702 ± 0.044, SVM 0.716 ± 0.047. PR-AUC mean ± SD was LR 0.218 ± 0.056, RF 0.188 ± 0.047, GB 0.192 ± 0.051, SVM 0.191 ± 0.045. Full fold results and bootstrap intervals are reported in S4 Table.

The held-out ROC-AUC percentile intervals were LR 0.718–0.842, RF 0.687–0.832, GB 0.679–0.819, SVM 0.620–0.771. SVM recall and precision intervals at the 0.5 cut-off were degenerate at zero because the fixed model made no positive predictions. This does not establish zero uncertainty about performance at other cut-offs or in a new population.

After Holm correction, the significant DeLong comparisons were LR versus SVM (ROC-AUC difference 0.087; adjusted p = 0.001940); RF versus SVM (ROC-AUC difference 0.066; adjusted p = 0.040512). No matched-burden McNemar comparison remained significant after correction. The SVM probability and margin rules differed on 131 records (agreement 0.831). The probability rule produced TP/FP/FN = 0/0/51, whereas the positive-margin rule produced 19/112/32. SVC probability=True produces Platt-scaled probability outputs, and the 0.5 probability rule does not coincide with the sign of the SVM decision function in this fitted model.

In the RandomOverSampler sensitivity arm, held-out ROC-AUC/PR-AUC were LR 0.791/0.209, RF 0.758/0.242, GB 0.746/0.226, SVM 0.656/0.180. The sensitivity arm did not replace the primary balanced-weighting results (S5 Table).
